review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Metal halide perovskite light-emitting diodes have exhibited great potential for the next-generation
displays. However, the realization of highly efficient and bright pure-blue devices with narrow
emission bandwidth remains a significant challenge. Herein, we propose a controllable crystal
facet growth to diminish random crystal facet-correlated defects and reveal the underlying
mechanism of energy-driven facet-selective crystal growth. This strategy enables high-quality
pure-blue emitters with high crystallinity, low defects, and large exciton binding energy.
Consequently, we achieve highly performing pure-blue devices with a narrow emission bandwidth
of 14 nm, an external quantum efficiency of 14.0% at 1,699 cd m-2, and an impressive peak
brightness of 8,334 cd m-2 at an emission of 473 nm. We verify a good applicability of the strategy
in achieving high-performance sky-blue devices with a narrow emission of 15 nm, a high
efficiency of 23.8%, and a large luminance of 13,230 cd m-2 at 488 nm.

---

## Introduction

Metal halide perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) have garnered substantial attention in
next-generation display technologies due to their featured characteristics, including narrow
emission, high luminance, wide color gamut, and low-cost solution-processable fabrication.1-6
Remarkable progress has been made in green, red, and near-infrared PeLEDs,2,7-10 with their
external quantum efficiencies (EQE) comparable to those of quantum dot light-emitting diodes
(QLEDs) and organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs).11-13 Regrettably, blue PeLEDs, especially
pure-blue devices (<475 nm), merely present moderate performance,14-17 remaining inferior to that
of their green and red counterparts. More critically, broad emission bandwidths exceeding 25 nm
are frequently reported in current blue PeLEDs.14,18-20 These issues restrict the practical application
of PeLEDs in displays.

The popular blue-emissive perovskites consist of CsPbBr Cl colloidal nanocrystals,21,22 quasi-
x 3-x
two-dimensional (quasi-2D) perovskites,14,18,23-25 and three-dimensional (3D) bromide-chloride
mixed perovskites26-29. In the low-dimensional perovskite systems of colloidal nanocrystals and
quasi-2D perovskites, there is a concern of the poor charge transport in the perovskites due to the
presence of massive insulating ligands and/or large organic cations. Meanwhile, the wide phase
distribution in quasi-2D perovskites is extensively observed to induce broad emissions for the
PeLEDs.30-32 Instead, the 3D perovskites with high charge mobility, relatively fixed component,
and high Auger recombination threshold are promising candidates for achieving efficient, bright,
and narrowband blue PeLEDs.26,27 However, pure-blue emissive 3D perovskites usually suffer
from severe halide heterogeneity and high defect density during perovskite film preparation, which
prohibits further improvements in device performance. Encouragingly, the halide heterogeneity in
mixed bromide-chloride perovskites has been well addressed with the effective strategies, such as
vapor-assisted crystallization (VAC) treatment27 and cationic surfactant additives33.

Nevertheless, the performance of the pure-blue PeLEDs is still hindered by the presence of massive
defects (e.g., halogen vacancy defect). To minimize the defect density of 3D perovskites, organic
halide salts have been extensively employed to saturate the vacancy defects by post-treatment of
the crystallized perovskites34,35. Very recently, an all-site alloy method has been reported to
facilitate sequential A-site doping growth for high-quality formamidinium and cesium hybrid
perovskite with less trap density26. However, the fundamentally disordered crystal growth with
random facets during perovskite crystallization has not yet been solved. While the crystal facet has
been demonstrated to strongly correlate with the generation of trap states36. For example, Tao et
al. exhibited that the perovskite (111) facet has the highest defect density, whereas the perovskite
(100) facet has the least defects37. Similarly, Etheridge et al. showed the significantly enhanced
device performance by diminishing the (111) facet defects of perovskites38. Meanwhile, the (100)
facet was reported to have an excellent optical property with efficient carrier radiative
recombination39. As shown above, the crystal facet-correlated defects in the perovskites result in a
strong dependence of the device performance on the crystal facets. Therefore, the manipulation of
perovskite growth with desired crystal facets is essential to achieve high-quality perovskites and
thus high-performance devices.

In this work, we propose an effective approach of bis(3-aminopropyl)polyethylene glycol
(BAPEG)-assisted perovskite crystal oriented growth with preferred (100) and (200) crystal facets.
We reveal the mechanism of this facet-selective crystal growth by clarifying the energy-driven
selective adsorption of BAPEG on specific perovskite facets. The desired crystal facets promote
high-quality pure-blue perovskites by reducing more than 78% of the density of trap states.
Meanwhile, we also demonstrate a large enhancement in exciton binding energy for BAPEG-based
perovskites. Consequently, we report highly performing pure-blue PeLEDs with a narrow emission
bandwidth of merely 14 nm, a remarkable external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 14.0% at 1,699
cd m-2, and an impressive brightness of 8,334 cd m-2 among the best-performing pure-blue PeLEDs
based on 3D perovskites. Moreover, the devices exhibit an excellent lifetime of 45.7 min at 100 cd
m-2 and a consistent EL peak during operation and lifetime tests. In addition, our strategy is
applicable for high-performance sky-blue devices, where a narrow emission of 15 nm, a
remarkable efficiency of 23.8%, and a large luminance of 13,230 cd m-2 have been achieved. The
results manifest an effective approach for achieving efficient and bright pure-blue PeLEDs.
Particularly, the peak EQE is achieved at high brightness, which breaks through the extensively
reported high efficiency at low brightness, suggesting a great potential for practical applications.

---

## Results

Controllable crystal growth strategy. The control pure-blue (Cs/Rb/FA)Pb(Cl/Br) perovskites
with a regular three-dimensional structure were fabricated by spin-coating the perovskite
precursors dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), followed by a typical vapor-assisted
crystallization treatment for improved compositional homogeneity.27 After that, the perovskites
were annealed at 80 °C for 10 min to promote the crystal growth and remove the residual solvent.
For the target perovskites, the Bis(3-aminopropyl)polyethylene glycol (BAPEG) was employed to
treat the wet perovskites by spin-coating BAPEG solution (dissolved in chlorobenzene) before the
annealing process. Details are shown in the experimental section. As shown in the scanning
electron microscopy (SEM) images (Fig. 1a, b, Supplementary Fig. 1), distinct variations of the
film morphology are observed between the control and target perovskites. The control perovskites
have a typical island-like morphology with random crystal facets, as verified by X-ray diffraction
(XRD) measurements (Fig. 1c), where the characteristic diffraction peaks of (100), (110), (111),
and (200) facets are clearly observed. Differently, the target perovskites exhibit single crystal-like
morphology with regular crystal grains and dominant facets (Fig. 1b). While no variation of the
perovskite morphology after chlorobenzene treatment verifies the important role of BAPEG in
modulating the perovskite growth (Supplementary Fig. 2). The diffraction signals of (110) and
(111) planes are significantly weakened in the target perovskites, being accompanied by the
appearance of the sharp and strong diffraction peaks of (100) and (200) planes with nearly 5.5-fold
higher peak intensity than the control ones (Fig. 1c), which indicates the dominant (100) and (200)
facets in the target perovskites with high crystal quality. Sequentially, the crystal facet orientations
of the control and target perovskites were further detected by grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray
scattering (GIWAXS) measurement (Supplementary Fig. 3). The control perovskites exhibit a
weak diffraction ring at q = 1.1 Å−1, indicating the random orientations of (100) facet thus the
randomly oriented perovskite crystals (Fig. 1d).40 Conversely, the stronger discrete pattern of (100)
facet along q axis was observed for the target perovskites, showing the enhanced crystallinity with
preferential parallel lattice plane to the substrate (Fig. 1e).

To investigate the underlying mechanism of the distinct variation in crystal facet for the target
perovskites, theoretical simulations based on density functional theory (DFT) calculations were
performed to estimate the adsorption energy (E ) of BAPEG on different perovskite facets. The
ads
molecular structure of BAPEG is shown in Fig. 1f, which consists of the functional groups of ether
bond (C−O) and terminated amino (−NH ) with an average molecular weight (Mn) of ~ 1,500. The
2
degree of polymerization (n) of BAPEG was selected as one to simplify the calculation. The
electrostatic forces between the functional groups of BAPEG and the lead-halide complex of the
perovskites, including coordination and hydrogen bonding interactions, induce the spontaneous
adsorption of BAPEG on the (100), (110), and (111) facets of the perovskites, as verified by the
differential charge density images (Supplementary Fig. 4). The calculated adsorption energies for
BAPEG on the (100), (110), and (111) facets are −0.518, −0.707, and −0.763 eV, respectively (Fig.
1g). The larger E on the (110) and (111) facets than that on (100) facet indicates the
ads
thermodynamically favorable adsorption of BAPEG on the (110) and (111) facets. The large
adsorption energy of BAPEG on (110) and (111) facets derives from the strong coordination
interaction between BAPEG and the perovskites. Since the (110) and (111) facets have smaller
halogen vacancy formation energy than that for (100) facet (Fig. 1h, Supplementary Fig. 5), this
suggests the easier formation of halogen vacancy on (110) and (111) facets. The resultant halogen
vacancy provides massive uncoordinated Pb sites for the favorable adsorption of BAPEG.
Meanwhile, there are rich Pb atoms exposed on the (110) and (111) facets of the perovskites41, as
clearly shown in their top views (Fig. 1i), which further favors the adsorption of BAPEG. The
steric hindrance effect from the long chain of the BAPEG would inhibit the diffusion of the
perovskite precursor ions to the (110) and (111) crystal facets, thus diminishing the crystal growth
of these facets (Supplementary Fig. 6). As a result, more precursor ions easily diffuse and attach
to the (100) crystal facet, thereby promoting the crystal growth along such facet. Encouragingly,
the large defect formation energy for the (100) facet (Fig. 1h) would contribute to a great reduction
of the trap state density for the target perovskites, as discussed later. Consequently, the remarkable
variation in film morphology, dramatic improvement in the perovskite crystallinity, and distinctive
orientation in crystal growth contribute to the uniqueness and effectiveness of our approach to
conventional additive-assisted modulation of perovskite crystallization and film formation. We
also reveal a different crystal growth mechanism of energy-driven facet-selective crystal growth
from the latent heat-induced cool interfacial layer-assisted crystal growth42 by accurately
modulating certain facet growth processes. The morphological changes from irregular and island-
like control perovskites to regular and single crystal-like high-quality target perovskites contribute
to good crystal stability (Supplementary Fig.7), as well as high device performance shown in the
following part.

Photocarrier recombination dynamics. The time-resolved emission spectra (TRES) were first
performed to probe the photocarrier relaxation process in the perovskites. As shown in Fig. 2a, b,
both the control and target perovskites exhibit the strongest emission and longest lifetime at a
centered wavelength of around 473 nm, indicating a dominant band-to-band radiative
recombination within the perovskites43. While the target perovskites show a much longer lifetime
decay process than that of control perovskites (Fig. 2b), this benefits from the suppressed trap
states. We further extracted the time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) decay process of the
perovskites to directly present the photocarrier recombination dynamics (Fig. 2c) and fitted the
decay curves by a bi-exponential function. The fast and slow decay components of τ and τ relate
1 2
to the trap-assisted non-radiative recombination and radiative recombination, respectively.44 The
τ and τ values of 0.94 and 8.66 ns for target perovskites are much longer than 0.62 and 5.10 ns
1 2
of control perovskites (Supplementary Table 1). The prolonged lifetime for target perovskites has
been further verified by the TRPL spectra under different excitation intensities (Supplementary
Fig. 8), where the target perovskites show much longer lifetimes than that of control perovskites
at the same excitation power. These results suggest the efficient suppression of trap states for more
radiative recombination in the target perovskites.

The ultrafast transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy was further carried out to reveal the
photogenerated carrier recombination dynamics in the control and target perovskites. The TA
spectra of the perovskites at different timescales are recorded in Fig. 2d, e. Both the control and
target perovskites show a distinctive photobleaching (PB) peak located at around 470 nm, which
is attributed to the ground-state bleaching signal, being consistent with their steady-state
absorption spectra (Supplementary Fig. 9). It is observed that the PB peaks gradually decrease
with prolonging the decay time, indicating the photogenerated carrier recombination process. To
clearly clarify the carrier recombination process, time traces of the PB peaks are extracted in Fig.
2f. The decay curve of the target perovskites exhibits a slower decay rate than that of the control
perovskites. Accordingly, the fitting analysis reveals significantly prolonged decay components
for the target perovskites (Supplementary Table 2), indicating a lower defect density for enhanced
radiative recombination, which is well consistent with the TRPL results. Moreover, the trap state
densities of the perovskites are quantized by the space charge-limited current measurements
(Supplementary Fig. 10), where the trap-filled limit voltage (V ) is proportional to the density of
TFL
trap states (N). The calculated N for the target perovskites is 9.79 × 1016 cm−3, which is reduced
t t
by more than 78% from 4.50 × 1017 cm−3 of the control perovskites.

Besides, the strong carrier radiative recombination for the target perovskites was further verified
by the temperature-dependent PL measurements (Fig. 2g, h). We monitored the perovskite PL
spectra from 80 K to 300 K, and exhibited a declined PL intensity by elevating the temperature,
deriving from the increased electron-phonon interaction and lattice expansion at high
temperatures45. We show more radiative recombination within the target perovskites than control
perovskites by observing a stronger PL peak intensity at the same temperature. We further
extracted the exciton binding energy (E ) of the perovskites from the fitting curves (Fig. 2i) based
b
on the equation of I =I /(1+A exp(−E /(k T)), where I , A, and k represent the integrated PL
T 0 b B 0 E B
intensity at 0 K, a coefficient, and Boltzmann constant, respectively.46 The obtained E for the
b
target perovskites is 55.2 meV, which is larger than 40.7 meV for the control perovskites, thus
favoring the inhibition of exciton dissociation and leading to more radiative recombination.
Consistently, we observe an over 2-fold higher photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQY) from
18.6% to of 41.5% for the target perovskites under different excitation intensities (Supplementary
Fig. 11). The increased E of the target perovskites can be ascribed to the enhanced dielectric
b
confinement by the adsorption of BAPEG on the perovskite surface (Supplementary Fig. 10c).
Consequently, we have exhibited strong radiative recombination of the photocarriers in the target
perovskites, benefiting from the large reduction in trap state density and the significant increase in
exciton binding energy, thereby promoting high emission efficiency in the devices, as will be
discussed later.

Interaction with the perovskites. We further demonstrated a strong interaction between BAPEG
and the perovskites (mainly the lead-halide complex). To directly show the interaction between
BAPEG and the lead-halide complex, the Raman spectra were first performed on BAPEG and
BAPEG-treated Pb(Br/Cl) powder (BAPEG-Pb(Br/Cl) ). As shown in Fig. 3a, a distinct Raman
2 2
peak located at 143.4 cm-1, being attributed to the characteristic signal of Pb−O bond47, is observed
for BAPEG-Pb(Br/Cl) . This signal is absent in the Raman spectra of either BAPEG or Pb(Br/Cl) ,
2 2
indicating an interaction between O in BAPEG and Pb2+ in Pb(Br/Cl) . To further confirm the
2

5/2 7/2
binding energies of 142.3 and 137.4 eV for the target perovskites. The low binding energy indicates

3/2 5/2

2

2

2

x

Supplementary Table 4). Notably, the high efficiency of 14.0% is achieved at a high brightness of
1,699 cd m-2, which breaks the conventional pattern of the peak efficiency generally obtained at
low brightness for blue PeLEDs, indicating promising candidates for the practical application in

of 5,273 cd m-2 and a peak efficiency of 6.7%, which are comparable to those of the pristine devices
reported previously26,28,34. The average efficiency extracted from 20 devices for the target PeLEDs
is 11.8% (Fig. 4g), which is much higher than 5.7% of the control devices. Besides, we also
demonstrate a good applicability of our strategy in achieving high-performance sky-blue PeLEDs
with a very narrow emission bandwidth of 15 nm among the state-of-the-art sky-blue devices
(Supplementary Table 5). Meanwhile, great enhancements in efficiency and luminance from 16.7%
and 11,926 cd m-2 to 23.8% and 13,230 cd m-2 are achieved for the sky-blue devices
(Supplementary Fig. 16). Particularly, the devices show a remarkably high efficiency of 11.5% at
the peak luminance of 13,230 cd m-2 and 15.4% at a luminance of ~10,000 cd m-2, which is largely
higher than previously reported ones with efficiencies lower than 10% at peak luminance and/or a
luminance of 10,000 cd m-2. Furthermore, we demonstrate excellent operational and spectral
stability for the target PeLEDs. The lifetime (T , defined as the elapsed time of PeLEDs decaying
50
to 50% of the initial luminance (L )) of the target PeLEDs is 45.7 min at an initial luminance of
0
100 cd m-2 (Fig. 4h, Supplementary Fig. 17), which is over 6-fold longer than 7.2 min of the control
devices. Moreover, the EL peak position and the CIE y coordinate of the target PeLEDs remains
constant during the lifetime test (Fig. 4i, Supplementary Fig. 18), benefiting from the significantly

Besides, we also exhibit constant EL peak under various bias voltages for the target PeLEDs
(Supplementary Fig. 20), verifying the excellent spectral stability during operation. Consequently,
we achieve highly performing pure-blue PeLEDs with a considerably narrow emission bandwidth
of merely 14 nm among the state-of-the-art pure-blue PeLEDs. The remarkable efficiency and
brightness, as well as the excellent operational and spectral stability, enable our devices to be the
best-performing pure-blue 3D perovskite-based devices.

## Methods

Materials and chemicals. Cesium bromide (CsBr, 99.999%), lead bromide (PbBr , 99.999%),
2
lead chloride (PbCl , 99.999%), and rubidium bromide (RbBr, 99.99%) were purchased from Alfa
2
Aesar. Formamidinium bromide (FABr, 99.99%) was purchased from Greatcell Solar Materials.
Poly(9-vinylcarbazole) (PVK), 1,3,5-benzinetriyl-tris(1-phenyl-1-H-benzimidazole) (TPBi), and
LiF (99.99%) were purchased from Luminescence Technology Corp. Bis (3-aminopropyl)
polyethylene glycol (BAPEG), 4,7,10-trioxa-1,13-tridecanediamine (TTDDA), anhydrous
dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF) were purchased from Sigma-
Aldrich.

Preparation of perovskite films. The pure-blue perovskite precursor solution was prepared by
dissolving CsBr, RbBr, FABr, PbBr , PbCl , and TTDDA at a molar ratio of 1.1: 0.2: 0.2: 0.275:
2 2
0.725: 0.1 in DMSO, where the concentration of Pb cation was 0.13 M. The above precursors with
a ratio of 1.1: 0.2: 0.2: 0.44: 0.56: 0.1 was prepared for the sky-blue perovskites. The precursor
solution was stirred in a nitrogen-filled glovebox at 80 °C for 12 h, and then filtered through the
polytetrafluoroethylene syringe (0.2 μm) before use. The perovskite films were prepared by spin-
coating the precursor at 3,000 rpm for 60 s, followed by a vapor-assisted crystallization (VAC)
treatment for 1.5 min (i.e., the wet films were placed into a petri-dish (diameter: 60 mm) with 30
μL of DMF dropped before the sample placement). Then, the samples were annealed at 80 °C for
10 min to complete the control perovskite fabrication. For the target perovskite preparation, the
BAPEG solution (0.125 mg mL-1 in chlorobenzene) was spin-coated on the VAC-treated films at
3,000 rpm for 60 s, followed by an annealing process at 80 °C for 10 min.

Fabrication of devices. The indium tin oxide (ITO) substrates were successively washed with
deionized water, ethanol, and isopropanol. Then the substrates were dried with nitrogen and treated
with UV-ozone for 15 min. The NiO solution with a concentration of 20 mg mL-1 was spin-coated
x
on ITO substrates at 2000 rpm for 60 s, followed by an annealing process at 120 °C for 10 min to
obtain dense NiO films. Then the PVK solution (4 mg mL-1 in chlorobenzene) was spin-coated
x
on NiO at 3,000 rpm for 60 s and then annealed at 140 °C for 30 min. Then, the polyvinyl
x
pyrrolidone (PVP) solution (1 mg mL−1 in isopropanol) was spin-coated at 4,000 rpm and annealed
at 120 °C for 10 min to improve the wettability of the perovskite precursor on PVK. After the
substrate cooled down, the perovskite films were prepared by spin-coating the perovskite precursor
solution. Finally, the functional layers of TPBi, LiF, and Al electrode were sequentially evaporated
on the perovskite films to complete the device fabrication process.

Perovskite film and device characterization. The morphology of control and target perovskites
were detected by using the scanning electron microscope (Zeiss 1550). The XPS and UPS
measurements were carried out with a Thermo Fisher Escalab 250Xi instrument equipped with a
monochromatic Al K𝛼 radiation and an unfiltered He I (21.22 eVS) gas-discharge lamp. The XRD
patterns were obtained using an X-ray diffractometer of Bruker D8 Advance (Cu Kα radiation, λ
= 1.54 Å). The FTIR spectra were collected by using a FTIR spectroscopy (Thermo Scientific,
Nicolet iS10) in the range of 4,000 to 400 cm−1. Raman spectra were obtained through a micro-
Raman spectrometer (Horiba XploRA PLUS). The fluence-dependent PLQYs were detected using
an integrating sphere system equipped with an Edinburgh FLS1000 and a 405 nm CW laser. The
HAADF cross-sectional TEM samples were prepared using a dual-beam FIB system (Helios
Nanolab 600i, FEI) and the elemental mapping were captured on a Cs-corrected FEI Titan G2
TEM at 300 kV equipped with an integrated windowless Super-EDX system. GIWAXS
measurements were performed with a Xeuss 2.0 SAXS/WAXS laboratory beamline using a Cu X-
ray source and a Pilatus3R 300K detector. The device performances were recorded by an Ocean
Optics system equipped with a source meter (Keithley 2400), a spectrometer (QE Pro), and an
integrating sphere (FOIS-1). The lifetime of the devices was measured in a nitrogen-filled glove
box with the Ocean Optics system, which was calibrated with a radiometric calibration light source
(HL-3plus-CAL) before use. The devices were driven by a Keithley 2400 source meter, where a
constant current was applied to the devices lying on the top of the integrating sphere. The
brightness variation versus operation time was traced and recorded by a QE Pro spectrometer.

Transient spectroscopy. TRES spectra were acquired using an Edinburgh FLS 1000 fluorescence
spectrophotometer equipped with a picosecond pulse laser (365 nm) with a pulse width of 50 ps.
TA spectroscopy was obtained by using an ExciPro XL Femtosecond Transient Absorption Pump-
Probe Spectrometer (CDP systems). The samples were pumped with a femtosecond laser pulse
(365 nm), which was generated from an optical parametric amplifier. The probe pulses ranging
from 380 to 800 nm were derived from the fundamental 800 nm laser pulses with a small portion
(≈5 μJ) of a 2 mm thick CaF plate.
2

Calculations. The adsorption energy calculations based on density functional theory were
implemented with the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The generalized gradient
approximation proposed by Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) was selected for the exchange-
correlation potential. The cut-off energy of 480 eV for plane wave was set. The structures were
relaxed until the residual forces on the atoms declined to less than 0.05 eV Å-1 and a vacuum
spacing of 20 Å was applied perpendicular to the slab to avoid interlaminar interactions.

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, Chen et al. report Bis(3-aminopropyl)polyethylene glycol (BAPEG)–assisted crystal facet regulation to achieve efficient and bright pure-blue perovskite light-emitting diodes. The authors claim that the selective adsorption of BAPEG leads to preferential (100) and (200) crystal growth, reduced defect density, enhanced exciton binding energy, and consequently narrowband blue emission with high efficiency and stability.
However, compared with the previous work (Nat. Commun. 12, 361, 2021, Adv. Mater. 2021, 33, 2007169), this work appears to lack substantial novelty. The authors mainly reduced the vapour treatment time, which in turn lowered the performance of the control devices. The subsequent improvement achieved by introducing a surface treatment with BAPEG seems to passivate surface and bulk defects rather than demonstrating a fundamentally new mechanism or concept. Also, there are several inconsistencies and logical issues in the manuscript, making it not suitable for publication , the detailed concerns are given below:
1.There is too much overlap between this work and the previous work from Feng Gao’s group (Nat. Commun. 12, 361, 2021). Both works incorporated Rb+ and used vapour treatment to improve the performance of blue PeLEDs, and the perovskite compositions and device fabrication details are nearly identical. In the previous work, Feng et al. attributed the performance improvement to the vapor treatment, they also observe a more preferential crystal orientation along the (100) and (200) direction and enhancement of crystallinity with VAC-treatment. However, in this manuscript, the authors attribute it to the selective adsorption of BAPEG leads to preferential (100) and (200) crystal growth.
2.The reported EQE of 14% in this work is significantly lower than that of the best-reported pure blue perovskite LEDs (>20%), such as Sci. Adv. 2024, 10, eado5645; Adv. Mater. 2025, 37(42), e20131; ACS Energy Lett. 2025, 10, 3638; and Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 10621. Even the highlighted maximum brightness of 8,334 cd m⁻² is not particularly competitive compared with previous reports, for instance 8,136 cd m⁻² (ACS Energy Lett. 2023, 8, 2897-2903) and 29,800 cd m⁻² (ACS Nano 2025, 19, 16850–16858). Overall, both the EQE and brightness achieved in this work are not superior to the state-of-the-art results.
3.The key claims regarding “defect suppression” lack convincing experimental evidence. The estimated trap-state density differs by less than one order of magnitude in Supplementary Fig. 6 (4.34 × 1017 ~ 1.79 × 1017 cm−3), which does not convincingly support the page 8, lines 209 “the great reduction in trap state density” as claimed.
4.The authors believe that the PL lifetime is prolonged, suggesting a reduced trap-assisted non-radiative recombination. However, there is no clear difference in table S1 (3~7ns for the averaged lifetime). Also, the authors claim that the extracted decay lifetimes imply reduced defect density in target sample since the PL lifetime reflects the trap-assisted carrier recombination rates. However, carrier recombination rates depend on the inject carrier densities, the PL lifetime comparison between different samples should have been made at constant excitation density, and thus, dependence on laser fluence should be shown. If this is not the case, the inconsistency needs to be discovered critically to understand the photophysics mechanism.
5.It is a big claim that there is no EL shift during the lifetime measurements. The authors should provide the evolution of the CIE y coordinate as a function of time under a constant current condition. This measurement is essential to evaluate the EL stability of the device during lifetime measurement.
6.If the authors believe that the exciton binding energies are high, they should also measure the fluence-dependent photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) to evaluate the exciton recombination dynamics.
7.As shown in Fig. 1a and b, the control and target films exhibit markedly different morphologies. The target film displays smaller grain sizes and a higher density of voids. Such morphological differences may strongly influence the PLQY and PL lifetimes through surface-related effects. A discussion on how these morphological changes correlate with crystal and device stability would be valuable.
8.The authors attribute the observed shift of the Pb 4f binding energy to the coordination between oxygen atoms and Pb²⁺. However, this interpretation requires more rigorous justification. In XPS, a shift in the Pb 4f peak position can also arise from other possible interactions, such as coordination between amino groups (–NH₂) and Pb²⁺, or surface dipole effects. The authors should provide additional supporting evidence.
9.The authors attribute the positive shift of Br 3d and Cl 2p binding energies to hydrogen bonding interactions between halide ions and the N–H groups of BAPEG. However, this interpretation seems not convincing. A shift in binding energy alone cannot unambiguously confirm hydrogen bonding, as it can also originate from other factors such as changes in the local chemical environment, lattice contraction, compositional variation, or ionic incorporation. Additional evidence, such as FTIR, NMR, or DFT calculations, would be necessary to substantiate the claim of hydrogen bonding interactions.
10.It seems that the PL peak positions of the control and target samples appear inconsistent in Supplementary Fig. 5, with the control sample showing a redshifted PL emission, while in Supplementary Fig. 9 the EL peak positions of both samples are identical. Please provide a reasonable explanation.
11.Although the authors report improved device performance after BAPEG modification, it is unclear why the efficiency of their reference device is significantly lower than that reported in previous works (Nat. Commun. 12, 361, 2021) using same compositions and processing conditions. Notably, previous studies have achieved efficiencies of ~6% at 467 nm, and 11% at 477 nm, whereas the present device shows comparable efficiency (~6%) even at 473 nm. The authors are encouraged to clarify this discrepancy and discuss possible causes.
Some minor technical concerns:
1.The cross-sectional SEM image presented in Supplementary Fig. 7 lacks sufficient clarity, making it difficult to clearly resolve the device architecture.
2.Regarding the NIOX/PVK/Perovskite/TPBi/LiF/Al structure mentioned in this manuscript, please provide a reasonable explanation of how an identical perovskite precursor compared with previous related literature can be uniformly formed on the hydrophobic PVK layer surface without any modification.
3.Please provide references for all the data points in Figure 4g. The author should provide a thorough, up-to-date overview of recent advancements in pure-blue perovskite LEDs.

### Reviewer 2

In this work, the authors propose an interesting and novel approach to achieve facet-selective crystal growth and further reveal the underlying mechanism of energy-driven selective adsorption of BAPEG to specific perovskite facets. The resultant high-quality crystals enable fantastic pure-blue PeLEDs with an extremely narrow emission bandwidth of 14 nm at an emission of 473 nm, a remarkable efficiency of 14.0% at 1699 cd m-2, a high brightness of 8334 cd m-2, and excellent operational and spectral stability. These encouraging results support its publication in this journal after a couple of minor corrections.
1. The comparisons in emission bandwidth with the reported pure-blue PeLEDs should be further discussed to highlight the considerably narrow emission achieved in this work.
2. The high-quality perovskites may benefit the suppression of the ion migration process, which is considered as one of the important parameters to determine the device stability. The ion migration activation energy of the perovskites should be compared.
3. The target perovskites display an increased exciton binding energy (i.e., 55.2 meV vs. 40.7 meV), which benefits the inhibition of exciton dissociation for more radiative recombination. The reason for this enhancement needs to be clarified.
4. The perovskite emission layer shows a discontinuous crystal distribution on the substrates. Is there any leakage current in the devices by considering the probable direct contact between the electron and hole transport layers?
5. Illustrations of the perovskite crystal facet orientations are suggested to be included in Fig. 1 to visually show the orientation variations.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript presents a new strategy for preparing high-quality perovskite crystals by the manipulation of crystal facet growth. The mechanism of the facet-selective crystal growth has been partially clarified with both theoretical and experimental results. Moreover, pure-blue device performances with a narrow emission and high efficiency and stability have been demonstrated. Therefore, this manuscript might be considered for future publication after addressing all the following concerns.
1. Given the remarkable efficiency advances in pure-blue nanocrystals and quasi-2D PeLEDs, the manuscript should more clearly highlight the distinct advantages of 3D perovskites. Specifically, the issue of poor charge transport should be addressed with comparative mobility data, and the link between narrow emission spectra and 3D perovskites requires stronger justification, particularly compared with nanocrystal systems.
2. The morphological differences between control and target perovskite in Figures 1a and 1b are notable. While the facet-growth mechanism is proposed, it remains unclear whether the grain corner change stems from enhanced (111) facet growth or an alternative mechanism. A discussion of how adjacent facets interact and form corners during grain formation would be helpful.
3. The schematic illustration in Figure 1g looks a little weird. It looks as if the BAPEG molecules are randomly placed on the (1 1 0) and (1 1 1) surface without significant orientation and binding to perovskite surface. Are there any more reasonable absorption configurations? The author might need to check the electron density changes of BAPEG molecules to perovskite surface absorption and find out the exact interactions.
4. The adopted molecule of bis(3-aminopropyl)polyethylene glycol was dissolved in chlorobenzene. The potential impact of this solvent on perovskite morphology should be evaluated, with comparisons to alternative polar and non-polar solvents.
5. It is noted that the BAPEG treatment is applied to the perovskite films before the annealing. Is there any difference in the perovskite morphology of the BAPEG treatment after the annealing process?
6. The carrier mobility of the target perovskite films should be measured to verify the high-quality perovskite crystals after BAPEG treatment.
7. The energy levels of the target perovskite films are shown in the manuscript, while corresponding data for the control films should be included for comprehensive comparison.
8. The operational stability tests in Figure 4h should include concurrent voltage changes to better correlate performance decay with electrical behavior.

### Reviewer 4

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

## Paper

## Abstract

Metal halide perovskite light-emitting diodes have exhibited great potential for the next-generation
displays. However, the realization of highly efficient and bright pure-blue devices with narrow
emission bandwidth remains a significant challenge. Herein, we propose a controllable crystal
facet growth to diminish random crystal facet-correlated defects and reveal the underlying
mechanism of energy-driven facet-selective crystal growth. This strategy enables high-quality
pure-blue emitters with high crystallinity, low defects, and large exciton binding energy.
Consequently, we achieve highly performing pure-blue devices with a narrow emission bandwidth
of 14 nm, an external quantum efficiency of 14.0% at 1,699 cd m-2, and an impressive peak
brightness of 8,334 cd m-2 at an emission of 473 nm. We verify a good applicability of the strategy
in achieving high-performance sky-blue devices with a narrow emission of 15 nm, a high
efficiency of 23.8%, and a large luminance of 13,230 cd m-2 at 488 nm.

---

## Introduction

Metal halide perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs) have garnered substantial attention in
next-generation display technologies due to their featured characteristics, including narrow
emission, high luminance, wide color gamut, and low-cost solution-processable fabrication.1-6
Remarkable progress has been made in green, red, and near-infrared PeLEDs,2,7-10 with their
external quantum efficiencies (EQE) comparable to those of quantum dot light-emitting diodes
(QLEDs) and organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs).11-13 Regrettably, blue PeLEDs, especially
pure-blue devices (<475 nm), merely present moderate performance,14-17 remaining inferior to that
of their green and red counterparts. More critically, broad emission bandwidths exceeding 25 nm
are frequently reported in current blue PeLEDs.14,18-20 These issues restrict the practical application
of PeLEDs in displays.

The popular blue-emissive perovskites consist of CsPbBr Cl colloidal nanocrystals,21,22 quasi-
x 3-x
two-dimensional (quasi-2D) perovskites,14,18,23-25 and three-dimensional (3D) bromide-chloride
mixed perovskites26-29. In the low-dimensional perovskite systems of colloidal nanocrystals and
quasi-2D perovskites, there is a concern of the poor charge transport in the perovskites due to the
presence of massive insulating ligands and/or large organic cations. Meanwhile, the wide phase
distribution in quasi-2D perovskites is extensively observed to induce broad emissions for the
PeLEDs.30-32 Instead, the 3D perovskites with high charge mobility, relatively fixed component,
and high Auger recombination threshold are promising candidates for achieving efficient, bright,
and narrowband blue PeLEDs.26,27 However, pure-blue emissive 3D perovskites usually suffer
from severe halide heterogeneity and high defect density during perovskite film preparation, which
prohibits further improvements in device performance. Encouragingly, the halide heterogeneity in
mixed bromide-chloride perovskites has been well addressed with the effective strategies, such as
vapor-assisted crystallization (VAC) treatment27 and cationic surfactant additives33.

Nevertheless, the performance of the pure-blue PeLEDs is still hindered by the presence of massive
defects (e.g., halogen vacancy defect). To minimize the defect density of 3D perovskites, organic
halide salts have been extensively employed to saturate the vacancy defects by post-treatment of
the crystallized perovskites34,35. Very recently, an all-site alloy method has been reported to
facilitate sequential A-site doping growth for high-quality formamidinium and cesium hybrid
perovskite with less trap density26. However, the fundamentally disordered crystal growth with
random facets during perovskite crystallization has not yet been solved. While the crystal facet has
been demonstrated to strongly correlate with the generation of trap states36. For example, Tao et
al. exhibited that the perovskite (111) facet has the highest defect density, whereas the perovskite
(100) facet has the least defects37. Similarly, Etheridge et al. showed the significantly enhanced
device performance by diminishing the (111) facet defects of perovskites38. Meanwhile, the (100)
facet was reported to have an excellent optical property with efficient carrier radiative
recombination39. As shown above, the crystal facet-correlated defects in the perovskites result in a
strong dependence of the device performance on the crystal facets. Therefore, the manipulation of
perovskite growth with desired crystal facets is essential to achieve high-quality perovskites and
thus high-performance devices.

In this work, we propose an effective approach of bis(3-aminopropyl)polyethylene glycol
(BAPEG)-assisted perovskite crystal oriented growth with preferred (100) and (200) crystal facets.
We reveal the mechanism of this facet-selective crystal growth by clarifying the energy-driven
selective adsorption of BAPEG on specific perovskite facets. The desired crystal facets promote
high-quality pure-blue perovskites by reducing more than 78% of the density of trap states.
Meanwhile, we also demonstrate a large enhancement in exciton binding energy for BAPEG-based
perovskites. Consequently, we report highly performing pure-blue PeLEDs with a narrow emission
bandwidth of merely 14 nm, a remarkable external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 14.0% at 1,699
cd m-2, and an impressive brightness of 8,334 cd m-2 among the best-performing pure-blue PeLEDs
based on 3D perovskites. Moreover, the devices exhibit an excellent lifetime of 45.7 min at 100 cd
m-2 and a consistent EL peak during operation and lifetime tests. In addition, our strategy is
applicable for high-performance sky-blue devices, where a narrow emission of 15 nm, a
remarkable efficiency of 23.8%, and a large luminance of 13,230 cd m-2 have been achieved. The
results manifest an effective approach for achieving efficient and bright pure-blue PeLEDs.
Particularly, the peak EQE is achieved at high brightness, which breaks through the extensively
reported high efficiency at low brightness, suggesting a great potential for practical applications.

---

## Results

Controllable crystal growth strategy. The control pure-blue (Cs/Rb/FA)Pb(Cl/Br) perovskites
with a regular three-dimensional structure were fabricated by spin-coating the perovskite
precursors dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), followed by a typical vapor-assisted
crystallization treatment for improved compositional homogeneity.27 After that, the perovskites
were annealed at 80 °C for 10 min to promote the crystal growth and remove the residual solvent.
For the target perovskites, the Bis(3-aminopropyl)polyethylene glycol (BAPEG) was employed to
treat the wet perovskites by spin-coating BAPEG solution (dissolved in chlorobenzene) before the
annealing process. Details are shown in the experimental section. As shown in the scanning
electron microscopy (SEM) images (Fig. 1a, b, Supplementary Fig. 1), distinct variations of the
film morphology are observed between the control and target perovskites. The control perovskites
have a typical island-like morphology with random crystal facets, as verified by X-ray diffraction
(XRD) measurements (Fig. 1c), where the characteristic diffraction peaks of (100), (110), (111),
and (200) facets are clearly observed. Differently, the target perovskites exhibit single crystal-like
morphology with regular crystal grains and dominant facets (Fig. 1b). While no variation of the
perovskite morphology after chlorobenzene treatment verifies the important role of BAPEG in
modulating the perovskite growth (Supplementary Fig. 2). The diffraction signals of (110) and
(111) planes are significantly weakened in the target perovskites, being accompanied by the
appearance of the sharp and strong diffraction peaks of (100) and (200) planes with nearly 5.5-fold
higher peak intensity than the control ones (Fig. 1c), which indicates the dominant (100) and (200)
facets in the target perovskites with high crystal quality. Sequentially, the crystal facet orientations
of the control and target perovskites were further detected by grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray
scattering (GIWAXS) measurement (Supplementary Fig. 3). The control perovskites exhibit a
weak diffraction ring at q = 1.1 Å−1, indicating the random orientations of (100) facet thus the
randomly oriented perovskite crystals (Fig. 1d).40 Conversely, the stronger discrete pattern of (100)
facet along q axis was observed for the target perovskites, showing the enhanced crystallinity with
preferential parallel lattice plane to the substrate (Fig. 1e).

To investigate the underlying mechanism of the distinct variation in crystal facet for the target
perovskites, theoretical simulations based on density functional theory (DFT) calculations were
performed to estimate the adsorption energy (E ) of BAPEG on different perovskite facets. The
ads
molecular structure of BAPEG is shown in Fig. 1f, which consists of the functional groups of ether
bond (C−O) and terminated amino (−NH ) with an average molecular weight (Mn) of ~ 1,500. The
2
degree of polymerization (n) of BAPEG was selected as one to simplify the calculation. The
electrostatic forces between the functional groups of BAPEG and the lead-halide complex of the
perovskites, including coordination and hydrogen bonding interactions, induce the spontaneous
adsorption of BAPEG on the (100), (110), and (111) facets of the perovskites, as verified by the
differential charge density images (Supplementary Fig. 4). The calculated adsorption energies for
BAPEG on the (100), (110), and (111) facets are −0.518, −0.707, and −0.763 eV, respectively (Fig.
1g). The larger E on the (110) and (111) facets than that on (100) facet indicates the
ads
thermodynamically favorable adsorption of BAPEG on the (110) and (111) facets. The large
adsorption energy of BAPEG on (110) and (111) facets derives from the strong coordination
interaction between BAPEG and the perovskites. Since the (110) and (111) facets have smaller
halogen vacancy formation energy than that for (100) facet (Fig. 1h, Supplementary Fig. 5), this
suggests the easier formation of halogen vacancy on (110) and (111) facets. The resultant halogen
vacancy provides massive uncoordinated Pb sites for the favorable adsorption of BAPEG.
Meanwhile, there are rich Pb atoms exposed on the (110) and (111) facets of the perovskites41, as
clearly shown in their top views (Fig. 1i), which further favors the adsorption of BAPEG. The
steric hindrance effect from the long chain of the BAPEG would inhibit the diffusion of the
perovskite precursor ions to the (110) and (111) crystal facets, thus diminishing the crystal growth
of these facets (Supplementary Fig. 6). As a result, more precursor ions easily diffuse and attach
to the (100) crystal facet, thereby promoting the crystal growth along such facet. Encouragingly,
the large defect formation energy for the (100) facet (Fig. 1h) would contribute to a great reduction
of the trap state density for the target perovskites, as discussed later. Consequently, the remarkable
variation in film morphology, dramatic improvement in the perovskite crystallinity, and distinctive
orientation in crystal growth contribute to the uniqueness and effectiveness of our approach to
conventional additive-assisted modulation of perovskite crystallization and film formation. We
also reveal a different crystal growth mechanism of energy-driven facet-selective crystal growth
from the latent heat-induced cool interfacial layer-assisted crystal growth42 by accurately
modulating certain facet growth processes. The morphological changes from irregular and island-
like control perovskites to regular and single crystal-like high-quality target perovskites contribute
to good crystal stability (Supplementary Fig.7), as well as high device performance shown in the
following part.

(Supplementary Table 5). Meanwhile, great enhancements in efficiency and luminance from 16.7%
and 11,926 cd m-2 to 23.8% and 13,230 cd m-2 are achieved for the sky-blue devices
(Supplementary Fig. 16). Particularly, the devices show a remarkably high efficiency of 11.5% at

higher than previously reported ones with efficiencies lower than 10% at peak luminance and/or a
luminance of 10,000 cd m-2. Furthermore, we demonstrate excellent operational and spectral
stability for the target PeLEDs. The lifetime (T , defined as the elapsed time of PeLEDs decaying
50
to 50% of the initial luminance (L )) of the target PeLEDs is 45.7 min at an initial luminance of
0
100 cd m-2 (Fig. 4h, Supplementary Fig. 17), which is over 6-fold longer than 7.2 min of the control
devices. Moreover, the EL peak position and the CIE y coordinate of the target PeLEDs remains

## Methods

Materials and chemicals. Cesium bromide (CsBr, 99.999%), lead bromide (PbBr , 99.999%),
2
lead chloride (PbCl , 99.999%), and rubidium bromide (RbBr, 99.99%) were purchased from Alfa
2
Aesar. Formamidinium bromide (FABr, 99.99%) was purchased from Greatcell Solar Materials.
Poly(9-vinylcarbazole) (PVK), 1,3,5-benzinetriyl-tris(1-phenyl-1-H-benzimidazole) (TPBi), and
LiF (99.99%) were purchased from Luminescence Technology Corp. Bis (3-aminopropyl)
polyethylene glycol (BAPEG), 4,7,10-trioxa-1,13-tridecanediamine (TTDDA), anhydrous
dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF) were purchased from Sigma-
Aldrich.

Preparation of perovskite films. The pure-blue perovskite precursor solution was prepared by
dissolving CsBr, RbBr, FABr, PbBr , PbCl , and TTDDA at a molar ratio of 1.1: 0.2: 0.2: 0.275:
2 2
0.725: 0.1 in DMSO, where the concentration of Pb cation was 0.13 M. The above precursors with
a ratio of 1.1: 0.2: 0.2: 0.44: 0.56: 0.1 was prepared for the sky-blue perovskites. The precursor
solution was stirred in a nitrogen-filled glovebox at 80 °C for 12 h, and then filtered through the
polytetrafluoroethylene syringe (0.2 μm) before use. The perovskite films were prepared by spin-
coating the precursor at 3,000 rpm for 60 s, followed by a vapor-assisted crystallization (VAC)
treatment for 1.5 min (i.e., the wet films were placed into a petri-dish (diameter: 60 mm) with 30
μL of DMF dropped before the sample placement). Then, the samples were annealed at 80 °C for
10 min to complete the control perovskite fabrication. For the target perovskite preparation, the
BAPEG solution (0.125 mg mL-1 in chlorobenzene) was spin-coated on the VAC-treated films at
3,000 rpm for 60 s, followed by an annealing process at 80 °C for 10 min.

Fabrication of devices. The indium tin oxide (ITO) substrates were successively washed with
deionized water, ethanol, and isopropanol. Then the substrates were dried with nitrogen and treated
with UV-ozone for 15 min. The NiO solution with a concentration of 20 mg mL-1 was spin-coated
x
on ITO substrates at 2000 rpm for 60 s, followed by an annealing process at 120 °C for 10 min to
obtain dense NiO films. Then the PVK solution (4 mg mL-1 in chlorobenzene) was spin-coated
x
on NiO at 3,000 rpm for 60 s and then annealed at 140 °C for 30 min. Then, the polyvinyl
x
pyrrolidone (PVP) solution (1 mg mL−1 in isopropanol) was spin-coated at 4,000 rpm and annealed
at 120 °C for 10 min to improve the wettability of the perovskite precursor on PVK. After the
substrate cooled down, the perovskite films were prepared by spin-coating the perovskite precursor
solution. Finally, the functional layers of TPBi, LiF, and Al electrode were sequentially evaporated
on the perovskite films to complete the device fabrication process.

Perovskite film and device characterization. The morphology of control and target perovskites
were detected by using the scanning electron microscope (Zeiss 1550). The XPS and UPS
measurements were carried out with a Thermo Fisher Escalab 250Xi instrument equipped with a
monochromatic Al K𝛼 radiation and an unfiltered He I (21.22 eVS) gas-discharge lamp. The XRD
patterns were obtained using an X-ray diffractometer of Bruker D8 Advance (Cu Kα radiation, λ
= 1.54 Å). The FTIR spectra were collected by using a FTIR spectroscopy (Thermo Scientific,
Nicolet iS10) in the range of 4,000 to 400 cm−1. Raman spectra were obtained through a micro-
Raman spectrometer (Horiba XploRA PLUS). The fluence-dependent PLQYs were detected using
an integrating sphere system equipped with an Edinburgh FLS1000 and a 405 nm CW laser. The
HAADF cross-sectional TEM samples were prepared using a dual-beam FIB system (Helios
Nanolab 600i, FEI) and the elemental mapping were captured on a Cs-corrected FEI Titan G2
TEM at 300 kV equipped with an integrated windowless Super-EDX system. GIWAXS
measurements were performed with a Xeuss 2.0 SAXS/WAXS laboratory beamline using a Cu X-
ray source and a Pilatus3R 300K detector. The device performances were recorded by an Ocean
Optics system equipped with a source meter (Keithley 2400), a spectrometer (QE Pro), and an
integrating sphere (FOIS-1). The lifetime of the devices was measured in a nitrogen-filled glove
box with the Ocean Optics system, which was calibrated with a radiometric calibration light source
(HL-3plus-CAL) before use. The devices were driven by a Keithley 2400 source meter, where a
constant current was applied to the devices lying on the top of the integrating sphere. The
brightness variation versus operation time was traced and recorded by a QE Pro spectrometer.

Transient spectroscopy. TRES spectra were acquired using an Edinburgh FLS 1000 fluorescence
spectrophotometer equipped with a picosecond pulse laser (365 nm) with a pulse width of 50 ps.
TA spectroscopy was obtained by using an ExciPro XL Femtosecond Transient Absorption Pump-
Probe Spectrometer (CDP systems). The samples were pumped with a femtosecond laser pulse
(365 nm), which was generated from an optical parametric amplifier. The probe pulses ranging
from 380 to 800 nm were derived from the fundamental 800 nm laser pulses with a small portion
(≈5 μJ) of a 2 mm thick CaF plate.
2

Calculations. The adsorption energy calculations based on density functional theory were
implemented with the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). The generalized gradient
approximation proposed by Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) was selected for the exchange-
correlation potential. The cut-off energy of 480 eV for plane wave was set. The structures were
relaxed until the residual forces on the atoms declined to less than 0.05 eV Å-1 and a vacuum
spacing of 20 Å was applied perpendicular to the slab to avoid interlaminar interactions.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, Chen et al. report Bis(3-aminopropyl)polyethylene glycol (BAPEG)–assisted crystal facet regulation to achieve efficient and bright pure-blue perovskite light-emitting diodes. The authors claim that the selective adsorption of BAPEG leads to preferential (100) and (200) crystal growth, reduced defect density, enhanced exciton binding energy, and consequently narrowband blue emission with high efficiency and stability.
However, compared with the previous work (Nat. Commun. 12, 361, 2021, Adv. Mater. 2021, 33, 2007169), this work appears to lack substantial novelty. The authors mainly reduced the vapour treatment time, which in turn lowered the performance of the control devices. The subsequent improvement achieved by introducing a surface treatment with BAPEG seems to passivate surface and bulk defects rather than demonstrating a fundamentally new mechanism or concept. Also, there are several inconsistencies and logical issues in the manuscript, making it not suitable for publication , the detailed concerns are given below:
1.There is too much overlap between this work and the previous work from Feng Gao’s group (Nat. Commun. 12, 361, 2021). Both works incorporated Rb+ and used vapour treatment to improve the performance of blue PeLEDs, and the perovskite compositions and device fabrication details are nearly identical. In the previous work, Feng et al. attributed the performance improvement to the vapor treatment, they also observe a more preferential crystal orientation along the (100) and (200) direction and enhancement of crystallinity with VAC-treatment. However, in this manuscript, the authors attribute it to the selective adsorption of BAPEG leads to preferential (100) and (200) crystal growth.
2.The reported EQE of 14% in this work is significantly lower than that of the best-reported pure blue perovskite LEDs (>20%), such as Sci. Adv. 2024, 10, eado5645; Adv. Mater. 2025, 37(42), e20131; ACS Energy Lett. 2025, 10, 3638; and Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 10621. Even the highlighted maximum brightness of 8,334 cd m⁻² is not particularly competitive compared with previous reports, for instance 8,136 cd m⁻² (ACS Energy Lett. 2023, 8, 2897-2903) and 29,800 cd m⁻² (ACS Nano 2025, 19, 16850–16858). Overall, both the EQE and brightness achieved in this work are not superior to the state-of-the-art results.
3.The key claims regarding “defect suppression” lack convincing experimental evidence. The estimated trap-state density differs by less than one order of magnitude in Supplementary Fig. 6 (4.34 × 1017 ~ 1.79 × 1017 cm−3), which does not convincingly support the page 8, lines 209 “the great reduction in trap state density” as claimed.
4.The authors believe that the PL lifetime is prolonged, suggesting a reduced trap-assisted non-radiative recombination. However, there is no clear difference in table S1 (3~7ns for the averaged lifetime). Also, the authors claim that the extracted decay lifetimes imply reduced defect density in target sample since the PL lifetime reflects the trap-assisted carrier recombination rates. However, carrier recombination rates depend on the inject carrier densities, the PL lifetime comparison between different samples should have been made at constant excitation density, and thus, dependence on laser fluence should be shown. If this is not the case, the inconsistency needs to be discovered critically to understand the photophysics mechanism.
5.It is a big claim that there is no EL shift during the lifetime measurements. The authors should provide the evolution of the CIE y coordinate as a function of time under a constant current condition. This measurement is essential to evaluate the EL stability of the device during lifetime measurement.
6.If the authors believe that the exciton binding energies are high, they should also measure the fluence-dependent photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) to evaluate the exciton recombination dynamics.
7.As shown in Fig. 1a and b, the control and target films exhibit markedly different morphologies. The target film displays smaller grain sizes and a higher density of voids. Such morphological differences may strongly influence the PLQY and PL lifetimes through surface-related effects. A discussion on how these morphological changes correlate with crystal and device stability would be valuable.
8.The authors attribute the observed shift of the Pb 4f binding energy to the coordination between oxygen atoms and Pb²⁺. However, this interpretation requires more rigorous justification. In XPS, a shift in the Pb 4f peak position can also arise from other possible interactions, such as coordination between amino groups (–NH₂) and Pb²⁺, or surface dipole effects. The authors should provide additional supporting evidence.
9.The authors attribute the positive shift of Br 3d and Cl 2p binding energies to hydrogen bonding interactions between halide ions and the N–H groups of BAPEG. However, this interpretation seems not convincing. A shift in binding energy alone cannot unambiguously confirm hydrogen bonding, as it can also originate from other factors such as changes in the local chemical environment, lattice contraction, compositional variation, or ionic incorporation. Additional evidence, such as FTIR, NMR, or DFT calculations, would be necessary to substantiate the claim of hydrogen bonding interactions.
10.It seems that the PL peak positions of the control and target samples appear inconsistent in Supplementary Fig. 5, with the control sample showing a redshifted PL emission, while in Supplementary Fig. 9 the EL peak positions of both samples are identical. Please provide a reasonable explanation.
11.Although the authors report improved device performance after BAPEG modification, it is unclear why the efficiency of their reference device is significantly lower than that reported in previous works (Nat. Commun. 12, 361, 2021) using same compositions and processing conditions. Notably, previous studies have achieved efficiencies of ~6% at 467 nm, and 11% at 477 nm, whereas the present device shows comparable efficiency (~6%) even at 473 nm. The authors are encouraged to clarify this discrepancy and discuss possible causes.
Some minor technical concerns:
1.The cross-sectional SEM image presented in Supplementary Fig. 7 lacks sufficient clarity, making it difficult to clearly resolve the device architecture.
2.Regarding the NIOX/PVK/Perovskite/TPBi/LiF/Al structure mentioned in this manuscript, please provide a reasonable explanation of how an identical perovskite precursor compared with previous related literature can be uniformly formed on the hydrophobic PVK layer surface without any modification.
3.Please provide references for all the data points in Figure 4g. The author should provide a thorough, up-to-date overview of recent advancements in pure-blue perovskite LEDs.

### Reviewer 2

In this work, the authors propose an interesting and novel approach to achieve facet-selective crystal growth and further reveal the underlying mechanism of energy-driven selective adsorption of BAPEG to specific perovskite facets. The resultant high-quality crystals enable fantastic pure-blue PeLEDs with an extremely narrow emission bandwidth of 14 nm at an emission of 473 nm, a remarkable efficiency of 14.0% at 1699 cd m-2, a high brightness of 8334 cd m-2, and excellent operational and spectral stability. These encouraging results support its publication in this journal after a couple of minor corrections.
1. The comparisons in emission bandwidth with the reported pure-blue PeLEDs should be further discussed to highlight the considerably narrow emission achieved in this work.
2. The high-quality perovskites may benefit the suppression of the ion migration process, which is considered as one of the important parameters to determine the device stability. The ion migration activation energy of the perovskites should be compared.
3. The target perovskites display an increased exciton binding energy (i.e., 55.2 meV vs. 40.7 meV), which benefits the inhibition of exciton dissociation for more radiative recombination. The reason for this enhancement needs to be clarified.
4. The perovskite emission layer shows a discontinuous crystal distribution on the substrates. Is there any leakage current in the devices by considering the probable direct contact between the electron and hole transport layers?
5. Illustrations of the perovskite crystal facet orientations are suggested to be included in Fig. 1 to visually show the orientation variations.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript presents a new strategy for preparing high-quality perovskite crystals by the manipulation of crystal facet growth. The mechanism of the facet-selective crystal growth has been partially clarified with both theoretical and experimental results. Moreover, pure-blue device performances with a narrow emission and high efficiency and stability have been demonstrated. Therefore, this manuscript might be considered for future publication after addressing all the following concerns.
1. Given the remarkable efficiency advances in pure-blue nanocrystals and quasi-2D PeLEDs, the manuscript should more clearly highlight the distinct advantages of 3D perovskites. Specifically, the issue of poor charge transport should be addressed with comparative mobility data, and the link between narrow emission spectra and 3D perovskites requires stronger justification, particularly compared with nanocrystal systems.
2. The morphological differences between control and target perovskite in Figures 1a and 1b are notable. While the facet-growth mechanism is proposed, it remains unclear whether the grain corner change stems from enhanced (111) facet growth or an alternative mechanism. A discussion of how adjacent facets interact and form corners during grain formation would be helpful.
3. The schematic illustration in Figure 1g looks a little weird. It looks as if the BAPEG molecules are randomly placed on the (1 1 0) and (1 1 1) surface without significant orientation and binding to perovskite surface. Are there any more reasonable absorption configurations? The author might need to check the electron density changes of BAPEG molecules to perovskite surface absorption and find out the exact interactions.
4. The adopted molecule of bis(3-aminopropyl)polyethylene glycol was dissolved in chlorobenzene. The potential impact of this solvent on perovskite morphology should be evaluated, with comparisons to alternative polar and non-polar solvents.
5. It is noted that the BAPEG treatment is applied to the perovskite films before the annealing. Is there any difference in the perovskite morphology of the BAPEG treatment after the annealing process?
6. The carrier mobility of the target perovskite films should be measured to verify the high-quality perovskite crystals after BAPEG treatment.
7. The energy levels of the target perovskite films are shown in the manuscript, while corresponding data for the control films should be included for comprehensive comparison.
8. The operational stability tests in Figure 4h should include concurrent voltage changes to better correlate performance decay with electrical behavior.

(BAPEG)–assisted crystal facet regulation to achieve efficient and bright pure-blue perovskite
light-emitting diodes. The authors claim that the selective adsorption of BAPEG leads to
preferential (100) and (200) crystal growth, reduced defect density, enhanced exciton binding
energy, and consequently narrowband blue emission with high efficiency and stability.
However, compared with the previous work (Nat. Commun. 12, 361, 2021, Adv. Mater. 2021,
33, 2007169), this work appears to lack substantial novelty. The authors mainly reduced the

subsequent improvement achieved by introducing a surface treatment with BAPEG seems to

crystal facet-correlated defects of the 3D perovskites and yields high-quality pure-blue

morphology exhibit excellent tolerance to the environment erosion, where the PL

reasonable variation (~ 1 nm) after the test, indicating excellent stability against
environmental erosion.

Reviewer #3: The manuscript presents a new strategy for preparing high-quality perovskite
crystals by the manipulation of crystal facet growth. The mechanism of the facet-selective
crystal growth has been partially clarified with both theoretical and experimental results.
Moreover, pure-blue device performances with a narrow emission and high efficiency and
stability have been demonstrated. Therefore, this manuscript might be considered for future
publication after addressing all the following concerns.
R: Thank the reviewer for confirming the novelty of our work and the helpful comments.
C1: Given the remarkable efficiency advances in pure-blue nanocrystals and quasi-2D PeLEDs,
the manuscript should more clearly highlight the distinct advantages of 3D perovskites.
Specifically, the issue of poor charge transport should be addressed with comparative mobility
data, and the link between narrow emission spectra and 3D perovskites requires stronger
justification, particularly compared with nanocrystal systems.
R: Thanks for the valuable suggestion. The nanocrystals and quasi-2D perovskites are
very popular blue emitters for pure-blue PeLEDs, and significantly important works
have been done based on pure-blue nanocrystals (e.g., Adv. Mater. 37, e20131 (2025);
Sci. Adv. 10, eado5645 (2024)) and quasi-2D perovskites (e.g., Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.
64, e202513617 (2025); Adv. Mater. 37, 2409718 (2025)). These works greatly
promote the development of the pure-blue PeLEDs. However, compared with the low-
dimensional perovskite systems, the 3D perovskites have the advantages of high charge
mobility, relatively fixed component, and high Auger recombination threshold (Nat.
Commun. 16, 3254 (2025); Nat. Commun. 12, 361 (2021)), thus serving as very
promising candidates for achieving efficient, bright, and narrowband blue PeLEDs.
However, the issue of poor charge transport in the low-dimensional perovskite systems
has raised our concern due to the presence of massive insulating ligands and/or large
organic cations around the nanocrystals and quasi-2D perovskites. The extensively
reported carrier mobilities for blue emissive quasi-2D perovskites and nanocrystals are
~ 10-6 − 10-5 cm2 V-1 s-1 (e.g., quasi-2D perovskites: 3.4 × 10-6 cm2 V-1 s-1, ACS Nano
19, 39181 (2025); 7.5 × 10-5 cm2 V-1 s-1, Nat. Commun. 10, 1027 (2019) and
nanocrystals: 6.24 × 10-6 cm2 V-1 s-1, Light Sci. Appl. 11, 346 (2022); 1.09× 10-5 cm2 V-
1 s-1, Inorg. Chem. 62, 11665 (2023); 3.4 × 10-5 cm2 V-1 s-1, ACS Energy Lett. 10, 4518
(2025)). Instead, the 3D perovskites usually have relatively higher carrier mobilities of
~ 10-4 cm2 V-1 s-1 (e.g., 2.93 × 10-4 cm2 V-1 s-1 in this work).
In addition, the broad emission bandwidths exceeding 20 nm were frequently reported
for the quasi-2D perovskites and nanocrystal-based pure-blue PeLEDs (shown in Table
R2 below). In quasi-2D perovskites, the wide phase distribution is typically observed,
which accounts for broad emissions for the pure-blue PeLEDs. For the pure-blue
nanocrystal systems, it is a big challenge to obtain a very uniform size distribution. The
non-uniform size of the pure-blue QDs induces a broad emission for the devices. For
example, the large size distribution range of over 3 nm were extensively observed for
the small-sized CsPbBr nanocrystals with average sizes of ~ 3 − 10 nm, resulting in a
3
broad blue emission of over 20 nm (ACS Energy Lett. 8, 731 (2023); Small 20, 2400885
(2024); Adv. Mater. 37, e20131 (2025)). In addition, the emission bandwidth was
reported to further increase from 25 to 53 nm with enlarging the nanocrystal size
distribution range from ~ 5 to 20 nm (shown in Fig. R7 below).
For the 3D pure-blue perovskite emitters, the emission bandwidth is greatly influenced
by the halide homogeneity and the defect density. The halide heterogeneity in mixed
bromide-chloride perovskites has been well addressed by the effective strategies, such
as vapor-assisted crystallization (VAC) treatment, where the full-width at half-
maximum (FWHM) of ~18 nm could be achieved (Nat. Commun. 12, 361 (2021)). Very
encouragingly, we report high-quality 3D pure-blue perovskite emitters with single
crystal-like morphology for reduced trap state density. Subsequently, we further narrow
the emission bandwidth to merely 14 nm, representing the narrowest emission
bandwidth among the state-of-the-art pure-blue PeLEDs (Table R2 below). The result
shows an instructive approach of our work to achieve narrow emissive pure-blue
PeLEDs.

### Reviewer 1

Chen et al. report a high-performance perovskite LED by incorporating an additive molecule that is claimed to regulate crystal growth. However, the central premise—molecule/additive-assisted modulation of perovskite crystallization and film formation—has been extensively explored in the perovskite optoelectronics literature. As presented, the strategy appears incremental and lacks clear significance for the field. In particular, the proposed approach does not demonstrate sufficient novelty in light of prior reports (e.g., doi.org/10.1002/aenm.202506630; doi.org/10.1002/adom.202403012; doi.org/10.1002/aenm.202403965; Nano Lett. 2024, 24(35), 10972–10979; among others).
Moreover, the mechanistic basis for facet orientation during perovskite crystal growth has already been clearly established (e.g., Nature Synthesis 4, 1088–1094 (2025)). The manuscript does not convincingly differentiate its mechanistic insights from this existing understanding. At the molecular-design level, the selected additive also appears closely related to molecules reported previously (e.g., NH2-PEG5-NH2, ACS Nano 2025, 19(17), 16850–16858), further weakening the novelty claim.
Finally, the authors do not provide a rigorous, quantitative causal link between the claimed improvements in “crystal quality” and the enhanced EL efficiency. This point is important because high luminescence efficiency does not necessarily require highly crystalline or highly ordered films (for example, many high-performance OLEDs employ amorphous emitting layers). Without a clearer structure–property relationship and stronger evidence of distinct mechanistic contribution, I do not find the current work suitable for publication in Nature Communications and therefore cannot recommend acceptance.

### Reviewer 2

In the revised manuscript, the authors have well addressed all the reviewers' concerns and further improved the manuscript quality. The work is of great interest to the PeLED community, representing a significant advance in the field of perovskite based optoelectronic devices.. Therefore, I strongly recommend the publication of this work in Nature Communications.
